explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The burden says “…the eyes of men and of all the tribes of Israel are upon the LORD…” (Zechariah 9:1). Hadrach and Damascus are the first names on the list, and right away the message says where everybody is looking.

A king makes sense, since kings get a lot of looks. But the burden never names a king here. It says the eyes of men and of all the tribes of Israel are on the LORD (Zechariah 9:1). Keep that one in your apron pocket, because this chapter gets to a King soon enough.

Priests are easy to picture standing at the front. The verse doesn't say that, though. It says the eyes of men and of all the tribes of Israel are upon the LORD (Zechariah 9:1). Every eye in the verse is pointed at one place, and it isn't the priests.

Right on the money, friend. “Behold, the Lord will impoverish her…” (Zechariah 9:4). Tyre had silver like dust and gold like the dirt of the streets, and the Lord says He'll cast her wealth into the sea.

Tyre already had so much gold it was like street dirt, so you'd think more was coming. The verse goes the other direction. The Lord will impoverish her and cast her wealth into the sea (Zechariah 9:4). That's a lot of gold to lose, and I'd hate to be the one holding the net.

Tyre did build herself a fortress, so walls were on her mind. But the Lord doesn't say He'll guard them. He says she will be consumed by fire (Zechariah 9:4). The fortress is in the verse, and so is what happens to her.

I get it, a fortress sounds like it should handle anything. But the verse says the Lord will impoverish her and that she will be consumed by fire (Zechariah 9:4). The fortress is right there in verse 3, and the fire is still coming in verse 4.

Yes, friend. Tyre built a fortress and piled up silver and gold, but the verse says she will be consumed by fire (Zechariah 9:4). Walls and wealth are what she was counting on, and the text doesn't say they keep her safe.
You'd think a neighbor's loss might get a cheer. The verse says something else: “Ashkelon will see and fear…” (Zechariah 9:5). No party hats in this verse, baker.

That's it. When Ashkelon sees what happens to Tyre, the text says it will fear. Then Gaza will writhe in agony, and so will Ekron (Zechariah 9:5). This is a scared bunch of cities, and not one of them is celebrating.
That's right, friend. The verse says, “There will cease to be a king in Gaza…” (Zechariah 9:5). Gaza is one of the Philistine cities that goes through all this, and its king is part of it.
I can see why you'd think Gaza keeps its king. But the text says, “There will cease to be a king in Gaza…” (Zechariah 9:5). Gaza writhes in agony in the same verse, so it's a hard moment for her.
Yes, baker. “…I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.” (Zechariah 9:6). A mixed race will occupy Ashdod, and the verse then names pride as the thing being cut off.

A harvest is a reasonable guess, since it's something you can see and count. But the verse names something else. The LORD says, “…I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.” (Zechariah 9:6). The word is pride, and the harvest isn't mentioned.

Trade is a good guess after Tyre's silver and gold. The verse about Ashdod doesn't say that, though. The LORD says He will cut off the pride of the Philistines (Zechariah 9:6). Pride is the thing that gets cut.

That's the surprise, friend. “Then they too will become a remnant for our God…” (Zechariah 9:7). After the blood and the abominations are removed from their mouths, the Philistines are described as God's remnant.

After so much trouble in the chapter, a warning sounds natural. But the verse turns a corner. After the LORD removes the blood and the abominations, “…they too will become a remnant for our God…” (Zechariah 9:7). A remnant for God is a long way from a warning sign.

Tyre is the big name earlier in the chapter, so I see where that came from. The verse says nothing about serving her. It says the Philistines “…will become a remnant for our God…” (Zechariah 9:7). The remnant belongs to God, and Tyre doesn't come up.
Yes! The Philistines “…will become like a clan in Judah…” (Zechariah 9:7). They go from the burden list to being likened to a clan in Judah.

Egypt is a fair guess, since it's a big name in the Bible. But it isn't in this verse. The Philistines “…will become like a clan in Judah…” (Zechariah 9:7). Judah is the answer, and Egypt can go back in the pantry.
Assyria does turn up in other parts of the Bible, but not here. The verse says the Philistines “…will become like a clan in Judah…” (Zechariah 9:7). Judah is the name on this one.

explanations.answer: He keeps watch with His own eyes
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the verse, baker. “…never again will an oppressor overrun My people, for now I keep watch with My own eyes.” (Zechariah 9:8). The promise rests on the LORD watching with His own eyes, and the verse gives no other reason.

explanations.answer: Their walls will be too high
explanations.explanation: Walls feel like a natural reason, but the verse doesn't use it. It says never again will an oppressor overrun His people, “…for now I keep watch with My own eyes.” (Zechariah 9:8). Remember Tyre and her fortress, because this promise doesn't depend on walls.

explanations.answer: Their army will be too strong
explanations.explanation: The verse does mention an army, so I see the pull. But the reason given is something else. The LORD says, “…for now I keep watch with My own eyes.” (Zechariah 9:8). The promise isn't based on how strong their army is.
That's right. “Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem!…” (Zechariah 9:9). After all the burden talk, this is a big change of mood.

After all that burden talk, you'd expect more bad news. But verse 9 turns the mood right around. “Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem!…” (Zechariah 9:9). They're told to rejoice and shout in triumph.
You got it, baker. The King is “…humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” (Zechariah 9:9). A righteous and victorious King, and the verse puts Him on a donkey.

A victorious King on a war horse makes sense in a picture. But the verse says He is “…humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” (Zechariah 9:9). It even says donkey twice, in case anyone was hoping for a horse.

A golden chariot is about as fancy as it gets. But that's not what the verse says. The King is “…humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” (Zechariah 9:9). A chariot does come up in the next verse, and there the LORD says He will cut it off from Ephraim.
Yes, baker. “…the bow of war will be broken.” (Zechariah 9:10). The chariot and the horse are cut off, and the bow of war is broken.
Restringing a bow means you plan to use it again. But the verse says, “…the bow of war will be broken.” (Zechariah 9:10). Broken is a lot more final than restrung.
Putting a bow in storage sounds tidy. The verse is stronger than that. It says, “…the bow of war will be broken.” (Zechariah 9:10). Nobody is taking it down off the shelf later.
Yes! “Then He will proclaim peace to the nations.” (Zechariah 9:10). With the chariot cut off and the bow of war broken, the King's message is peace.

War is a fair guess when chariots and bows are in the verse. But they're being cut off and broken, and then He proclaims something else. “Then He will proclaim peace to the nations.” (Zechariah 9:10).

Judgment shows up in the first half of the chapter, so I see why it came to mind. But verse 10 says, “Then He will proclaim peace to the nations.” (Zechariah 9:10). The King's message to the nations is peace.

It sounds like a King of Jerusalem would stay near Jerusalem. But the verse goes far past that. “His dominion will extend from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” (Zechariah 9:10). Jerusalem's borders are just the start.

That's right. “His dominion will extend from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” (Zechariah 9:10). Jerusalem is only where He arrives on the donkey, and His dominion reaches to the ends of the earth.

That's it, baker. “As for you, because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.” (Zechariah 9:11). Because of the blood of His covenant, the prisoners are let out of the pit.

A waterless pit sounds like a place with no way out. But the verse promises the opposite. “…because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.” (Zechariah 9:11). The LORD says He will release them.

Babylon is a big name in the Bible, so I see why it came up. But this verse doesn't mention it. The LORD says, “…because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.” (Zechariah 9:11). Release is the word, and it's not a trip to Babylon.
That's right. “Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope…” (Zechariah 9:12). They aren't just released, they're told where to go.

It's easy to think the prisoners are released and then left to figure it out. But verse 12 gives them a direction. “Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope…” (Zechariah 9:12). They're told to return to their stronghold.
Yes, baker. “I will rouse your sons, O Zion, against the sons of Greece.” (Zechariah 9:13). The LORD has bent Judah as His bow, and now He rouses the sons of Zion.
Moab is a name you'll find elsewhere in the Bible, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD says, “I will rouse your sons, O Zion, against the sons of Greece.” (Zechariah 9:13). The sons are Zion's sons.
Edom turns up in other places in Scripture, but not in this one. The verse says, “I will rouse your sons, O Zion, against the sons of Greece.” (Zechariah 9:13). The answer here is Zion.

explanations.answer: The sword of a mighty man
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. “I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). First Judah was the bow, and now Zion is the sword.
A wall of bronze would be solid, no question. But the verse picks a weapon, not a wall. “I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). It's a sword.

A lion is a strong picture, and I see why you went there. But it isn't the one in this verse. “I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). The battle picture here is made of a bow and a sword.
That's right! “Then the LORD will appear over them, and His arrow will go forth like lightning.” (Zechariah 9:14). The LORD appears over them, and His arrow is likened to lightning.
Hail is a fair guess for something that falls from the sky. But the verse uses a different picture. “…His arrow will go forth like lightning.” (Zechariah 9:14). Lightning is the word.
A flood is big, but it isn't the picture in this verse. The verse says, “…His arrow will go forth like lightning.” (Zechariah 9:14). An arrow is fast, and so is lightning.
Yes, baker. “The LORD of Hosts will shield them.” (Zechariah 9:15). He sounds the ram's horn, and then He shields His people.
Scattering would be a sad turn, and the verse doesn't go there. It says, “The LORD of Hosts will shield them.” (Zechariah 9:15). The LORD is on their side here.

Going home does come up earlier in the chapter, when the prisoners are told to return to their stronghold (Zechariah 9:12). But this verse is about the battle. “The LORD of Hosts will shield them.” (Zechariah 9:15). The word here is shield.
That's right. “…they will be filled like sprinkling bowls, drenched like the corners of the altar.” (Zechariah 9:15). The people are likened to bowls that are full.

It's a strange picture, so I get the doubt. But the verse says, “And they will be filled like sprinkling bowls, drenched like the corners of the altar.” (Zechariah 9:15). The people are filled, and the verse says it plainly.
Sparkling right, baker! “…like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.” (Zechariah 9:16). Jewels are the picture of how His people will shine.
Feathers might look nice on a crown, but that's not what this verse says. “…like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.” (Zechariah 9:16). Jewels are what sparkle.
Flowers are pretty, and I can see why you picked them. But flowers don't sparkle, and jewels do. The verse says, “…like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.” (Zechariah 9:16).

After a battle you'd expect a tired bunch. But the chapter ends somewhere else. “How lovely they will be, and how beautiful! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine, the young women.” (Zechariah 9:17). Nobody is worn out in that verse.

Yes, friend. The last verse says, “How lovely they will be, and how beautiful! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine, the young women.” (Zechariah 9:17). They end up lovely and beautiful, and the chapter closes on that.
